Notes: c. 160 BCE. Year Established basis: earliest documented Jewish settlement at the site is the Oniad foundation. Snape: the temple at Tell el-Yehudieh was built by Onias "after his flight from Jerusalem around 160 BC", by permission of Ptolemy VI, and was "one of the centres in Egypt associated with resident Jewish communities during the Ptolemaic Period". (Identification of Tell el-Yahudiyeh with Leontopolis is disputed: Piotrkowski 2019 and Capponi 2025 place the temple elsewhere/Heliopolis.) Presence; no count.

Primary text: Josephus, Antiquities 13.3.1-3 (Ant. 13.62-73): Onias (IV) petitions Ptolemy VI Philometor and Cleopatra II to purify a ruined temple at a fortress in the "Nomus of Heliopolis" (Leontopolis) so "that those Jews which dwell in Egypt may have a place whither they may come and meet together"; Onias "built a temple, and an altar to God", smaller than Jerusalem's, and "found other Jews like to himself, together with priests and Levites" to serve there. Date only to the joint reign of Philometor and Cleopatra II (pre-145 BCE); c. 160 used. Founding of a Jewish priestly community; no number.

c. 150 BCE. Capponi (Il tempio di Leontopoli in Egitto, 2007, per BMCR review) follows Josephus' attribution to Onias IV, dating the temple "to shortly after Jonathan Maccabeus became High Priest in 152 BCE"; she argues "there was already a significant Jewish population in the area around Heliopolis before the temple was created" and that the community was predominantly Jewish soldiers. Evidence base: "just over 90 inscriptions that can be attributed to the site or to nearby Jewish settlements" (91 epitaphs, 12 in verse); no papyri. No population figure.

Mid-2nd century BCE (midpoint used). Encyclopaedia Judaica: "A settlement of Jewish soldiers was established in Leontopolis under the leadership of the former high priest" Onias IV, with the approval of Ptolemy Philometor and Cleopatra; the temple "served the Jewish inhabitants of the region for more than 200 years"; "Jewish inscriptions were found there"; the name Tell al-Yahudiyya "is a survival from this ancient Jewish settlement". Military colony; no count.

Earliest dated epitaph from the Jewish cemetery of Leontopolis (Tell el-Yahoudiya): Demas (JIGRE 30 / CIJ 1490), died aged about 38 "in the 54th (regnal year), Hathyr" of Ptolemy VIII = 117 BCE, leaving wife, young children and mother; possibly a communal leader (sophia). Askin notes Ameling instead proposes 24 CE. Individual Jewish resident; presence only.

c. 103-101 BCE (war of Cleopatra III vs. Ptolemy Lathyrus). Josephus, Antiquities 13.10.4 (Ant. 13.284-287), citing Strabo: Chelcias and Ananias, "the sons of that Onias who built the temple in the prefecture of Heliopolis", commanded Cleopatra III's army, and "only those that were called Onias's party, being Jews, continued faithful". Attests the Oniad military community; army size not given (and would not be resident population). Gruen (SCI 1997) doubts the father was the temple founder.

48/47 BCE. Josephus, Antiquities 14.8.1: "the Egyptian Jews, who dwelt in the country called Onion" at first blocked Antipater and Mithridates of Pergamum marching to relieve Caesar in Alexandria, then were won over by letters of the high priest Hyrcanus II and supplied the army; the Jews about Memphis followed. Shows a sizeable armed Jewish population in the Land of Onias (a district, not only the town). The 3,000 armed Jews were Antipater's Judean force, not residents. War 1.9.4 tells the same and a battle at the "Jews' Camp" (location uncertain).

c. 51 BCE-41 CE (midpoint). Askin (Henoch 43, 2021): "Twelve out of nearly ninety inscriptions at Leontopolis are metrical"; the necropolis is identified as Jewish by "many Jewish names", absence of Egyptian coffins, loculi tombs and the mound's name; "a third of Leontopolis epitaphs date to between mid-second century BCE to second century CE"; of over 120 Jewish epitaphs from Egypt "a majority are from Leontopolis", many dated to the 1st c. BCE/CE (Frey, CIJ II p. 381: about 51 BCE-41 CE). Literary and documentary evidence points "to a large Jewish community at Leontopolis". Presence of a large community; no count.

Early Roman period (63 BCE-70 CE; midpoint 4 used). Venit (Visualizing the Afterlife in the Tombs of Graeco-Roman Egypt, CUP 2015): Tel el-Yehoudieh was "a Jewish fortified city dating from the second century bce through the second century ce", "a predominantly Jewish establishment", styled "the land of Onias"; "more than eighty extant gravestones" (mid-2nd c. BCE to 2nd c. CE), all in Greek, "the second largest collection of inscriptions from the ancient Jewish Diaspora"; the epitaph of Arsinoe daughter of Aline and Theodosius calls her homeland "the land of Onias". Ages at death given (20, 53, 60). No population figure.

73 CE. Josephus, War 7.10.2-4 (War 7.420-436): after the Sicarii unrest in Egypt, Caesar ordered Lupus "to demolish that Jewish temple which was in the region called Onion" (built in a place 180 furlongs from Memphis in the Nome of Heliopolis); Lupus "shut up the temple itself" and his successor Paulinus stripped it and barred access; it had stood "three hundred and forty-three years". Closure of the temple; Josephus does not say the Jewish residents were removed, so Population blank (not 0).

73 CE. Capponi (per BMCR review): "the closure of the temple at Leontopolis by Vespasian in 73 CE was a propaganda measure" that "did not necessarily destroy the Jewish community around it"; "that community no doubt disappeared after the revolt of 115-17 CE" (outside period). Continued Jewish presence after the closure; no count.

c. end of 73 or early 74 CE. Modrzejewski (The Jews of Egypt, excerpted by COJS): Lupus governed 71-73 CE; "Paulinus succeeded him at the end of 73 or the beginning of 74. At that time the sanctuary was shut down permanently"; Lupus and Paulinus "contented themselves with stopping the services and closing the sanctuary" rather than demolishing it. End of the Oniad cult; no statement that Jews left the site.
